method: Complete candidate survey followed by individual editorial choices and written reasons, applied to the existing complete guide to keep it within 300 quotations. All verified authorized selections included. Priority given to foundational teachings, substantive explanations, necessary qualifications, distinctive applications, narrative examples and thematic breadth across an invitation that leaves the listener free, the effects of words and the capacity of the hearer, judgment through consultation, evidence and timing, courage joined to restraint and the repair of fellowship, directions given amid danger and changing circumstances, everyday encounters and common sense, patience before divine wisdom, and the closing accounts of tact and adaptation in service. Neither citation count nor source order used as a ranking rule. Imported wording checked separately; version differences remain explicit. The existing reading arc is retained.

selected.text: In the divine Tablets this word hath repeatedly been revealed: We have enjoined upon all the fear of God and that whereby stations and ranks are elevated. Blessed are they that act. One word setteth ablaze, and another extinguisheth.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh recalling that one word sets ablaze and another extinguishes, within a call to the fear of God and action; a compact form of the fire image.

selected.text: However, not every ear is worthy of every counsel and secret.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observing that not every ear is worthy of every counsel and secret; a short, memorable statement of discernment.

selected.text: Never talk about God to a man with an empty stomach. Feed him first
selected.reason: Reported saying of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá never to talk about God to a man with an empty stomach but to feed him first; a striking practical application of attention to need.

selected.text: The wise person sees the consequences of matters, not their beginnings.
selected.reason: Reported saying of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that the wise see the consequences of matters, not their beginnings; a concise statement of foresight.

selected.text: In all that we have borne there lies hidden a wisdom that none knoweth save God.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh saying that in all He has borne lies a wisdom none knows save God; a moving statement of hidden meaning in suffering.

selected.text: Discord is a consuming fire that must be quenched by the waters of wisdom and utterance.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh calling discord a consuming fire to be quenched by the waters of wisdom and utterance; a memorable image of reconciliation.

selected.text: The heaven of divine wisdom is illumined with two luminaries: consultation and compassion.
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: However, do not stay more than a week in any one place, so that it does not go beyond wisdom
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advising a traveler not to stay more than a week in any one place; a concrete travel direction.

selected.text: Do not write to the emperor; he is proud and preoccupied, and will not take heed at present.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advising not to write to a proud and preoccupied emperor who would not take heed; an example of judging receptivity and timing.

selected.text: Today is the day of mention and praise, but wisdom requireth that it be manifested in its proper time.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh saying that this is the day of praise but wisdom requires that it be manifested in its proper time; a concise statement on timing.

selected.text: You should act and behave according to wisdom and thought. What benefit is there in useless commotion?
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asking “What benefit is there in useless commotion?” and urging action guided by wisdom and thought; a short, memorable rebuke of agitation.

selected.text: By whatever means, work to calm his flame, show patience and forbearance, and exercise perfect wisdom.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asking that an angry person’s flame be calmed with patience, forbearance and perfect wisdom; a short practical counsel on de-escalation.

selected.text: With such people you must practice wisdom - never speak a word about the laws when conversing with them.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advising never to speak about the laws when conversing with certain people; a practical counsel on what to leave unsaid.

selected.text: speak to people according to their understanding. Argue not with them about their traditions and reasonings
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá bidding the friends speak to people according to their understanding and not argue with them about their traditions; a short counsel against contentious speech.

selected.text: Man has two ears and one tongue, so he should hear twice and speak once. The wise man listens much and speaks little.
selected.reason: Reported saying of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that man has two ears and one tongue, so the wise listen much and speak little; the saying the guide’s Proverbs reference relies on.

selected.text: However, in all matters they must observe wisdom and not accept claims from any soul merely on the basis of assertion.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh warning against accepting any soul’s claims on the basis of assertion alone; the caution against unchecked claims that the guide’s questions describe.

selected.text: You must be very careful that thieves do not steal your bag along the way. Be extremely, extremely vigilant and watchful.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá warning a traveler to be vigilant lest thieves steal his bag; a plain example of everyday prudence.

selected.text: When wisdom shines with spiritual radiance it becomes guidance, and when its lights beam upon the body it becomes medicine.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying that wisdom shining with spiritual radiance becomes guidance and on the body becomes medicine; a memorable image joining guidance and healing.

selected.text: As to thy coming at this time to the Blessed Spot (Acca), this is not in accordance with the wisdom revealed in the tablets.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advising that coming to ‘Akká at that time was not in accordance with wisdom; an example of a personal direction about pilgrimage.

selected.text: But fear God lest thou cause him temptation by speaking of these things. And if thou seest no good in him, turn away from him
selected.reason: The Báb warning not to tempt a hearer by speaking of certain things and to turn away if no good is seen in him; the Báb’s counsel on unreceptive listeners.

selected.text: The lamp of the horizons needeth oil that it may burn, but the divine lamp requireth the oil of heavenly wisdom that it may burn like a luminous torch. Praise be to
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying the divine lamp needs the oil of heavenly wisdom to burn like a torch; a memorable image of wisdom’s source.

selected.text: End. Keep these words concealed, for should he see them, he would become utterly hopeless, and this would be contrary to wisdom.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh asking that certain words be kept from one who would be made utterly hopeless by them; a distinctive example of wisdom as care for another’s heart.

selected.text: Follow ye wisdom under all conditions. He, verily, hath bidden all to observe that which hath been and will be of profit to them.

selected.text: The designation and promulgation of the Qiblih is not at present in accordance with consummate wisdom. It will be announced in due time.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying the designation of the Qiblih was not yet in accordance with wisdom and would be announced in due time; an example of timing in announcements.

selected.text: Were I to unravel the wondrous mysteries of Thy wisdom which are laid bare before me, the reins of Thine enemies would be cleft asunder.
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: Never let go of wisdom in any situation. It is not permissible to acknowledge matters which the ignorant are incapable of comprehending.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh forbidding acknowledgment of matters the ignorant cannot comprehend; a concise caution about capacity.

selected.text: If thou findest one who is receptive, rend asunder his veils with wisdom and utterance. Thus doth thy Lord, the All-Merciful, command thee
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh bidding the believer, when he finds a receptive soul, to rend its veils with wisdom and utterance; balances caution with bold teaching to the receptive.

selected.text: The ignorant always sees the present state while the wise looks to the future. I had no reproach for Jamal Pasha as I could see his end
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that the ignorant see the present while the wise look to the future, so He had no reproach for Jamal Pasha; a narrative example of foresight.

selected.text: Indeed, the wise seek to secure their rights through the acquisition of virtues, while the ignorant attempt to do this through compulsion.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that the wise secure their rights through virtues while the ignorant use compulsion; a sharp contrast between persuasion and force.

selected.text: Many events that occur appear to be accidental, but no, they are not accidental. Since that divine wisdom is hidden, it appears accidental.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that events seem accidental only because divine wisdom is hidden; a concise statement on providence.

selected.text: Although outwardly these cataclysmal disasters are hard to bear yet inwardly there lies a great wisdom behind them which will appear later.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that within outwardly hard disasters lies a great wisdom that will appear later; a statement of trust amid suffering.

selected.text: The friends must not act except with wisdom. Wisdom is that through which the servants draw nigh, not that which causeth remoteness and flight.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh defining wisdom as that through which people draw near, not that which causes remoteness and flight; a foundational definition used throughout the guide.

selected.text: But my Lord hath a supreme wisdom and His wisdom hath required the imprisonment of Abdul-Baha and the prevention of visits of impassioned friends.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying God’s supreme wisdom required His imprisonment and the prevention of visits; a personal example of accepting hardship.

selected.text: Warm and complete friendship with one of the pillars of the embassy as well as with respected merchants is necessary, for this accords with wisdom.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying warm friendship with an embassy official and respected merchants accords with wisdom; shows wisdom as building trust, not only concealment.

selected.text: In Qum, do not, for the time being, call that site by this name, but rather erect it in a different name, lest it cause dismay among the heedless
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directing that a site in Qum be given a different name for the time being, lest it cause dismay; a concrete example of wisdom about naming.

selected.text: When We commanded the people to wisdom, We concealed from them certain stations lest the fire of yearning wrest from their hands the reins of choice.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh explaining that certain stations were concealed lest the fire of yearning wrest the reins of choice from people’s hands; links divine concealment to human freedom.

selected.text: Whatsoever appeareth and cometh forth from the invisible realm into the realm of being hath been and is according to the requirements of divine wisdom.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh affirming that whatever comes into being does so according to divine wisdom; a concise statement of providence.

selected.text: Whatsoever may come to pass, be it tribulation or hardship, or ease and comfort, all transpireth according to the requirements of His consummate wisdom.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh saying that tribulation and ease alike transpire according to God’s consummate wisdom; a summary statement of the guide’s turn to divine wisdom.

selected.text: In all conditions observe wisdom and hold fast unto wisdom. In the blessed Tablets that which is revealed is contingent upon wisdom and limited by time.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh noting that what is revealed in the Tablets is contingent upon wisdom and limited by time; a necessary qualification for reading historical directions.

selected.text: And if the friends do hold meetings, they must be very discreet and hidden so that no commotion arises, for the people are weak and we must be forbearing.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asking that meetings be discreet so no commotion arises, for the people are weak and we must be forbearing; joins discretion and forbearance in gatherings.

selected.text: All these Prophets and Messengers were commanded to wisdom - that is, each spoke and revealed the Cause according to the capacity and measure of the people
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh explaining that all the Prophets were commanded to wisdom, each revealing the Cause according to the people’s capacity; places human tact within the pattern of revelation.

selected.text: However, it occurred without wisdom, and all are today commanded to act with wisdom. Although he thought he was acting according to wisdom, he was mistaken.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh noting of one who acted without wisdom that he thought he was acting wisely but was mistaken; an honest acknowledgment that sincere judgment can err.

selected.text: We counsel them and all the people of God to wisdom. Wisdom is like the sun for the new world, that is, the world of Baha, and it is a light for the nights.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh comparing wisdom to the sun for the new world and a light for the nights; a memorable image of wisdom’s place.

selected.text: there are souls who are not known outwardly but are known inwardly, as it says: "And a believing man from among Pharaoh's people who concealed his faith..."
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá noting that some souls are known inwardly though not outwardly, citing the believer of Pharaoh’s people who concealed his faith; a scriptural example of discreet faith.

selected.text: conditional fate may be likened to this: while some oil yet remains, a strong wind blows and extinguishes the lamp. This fate is conditional. It is expedient to avoid this fate, to guard oneself against it, and to be cautious and prudent
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: Therefore as the people cannot bear, consequently you should act with wisdom under all circumstances. Address ye the people according to their intelligences.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advising that, since people cannot bear everything, the friends should address them according to their intelligences; a concise instruction on capacity.

selected.text: Whatsoever appeareth hath not been, and is not, outside of divine wisdom. The people of insight and understanding have borne and do bear witness to this truth.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh affirming that nothing that appears lies outside divine wisdom, as people of insight bear witness; a concise statement of trust.

selected.text: If a soul truly looks to God's consummate wisdom in what He commands, he will certainly not move contrary to God's will, with complete contentment and submission.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh teaching that one who sees God’s consummate wisdom in His commands will follow them with contentment and submission; joins wisdom to trust.

selected.text: When thou desirest to enter among thy people, then manifest their Cause by thy Lord's leave, and speak not a word that would cause the people around thee to flee.
selected.reason: The Báb bidding the believer enter among his people and speak no word that would make those around him flee; the Báb’s counsel on drawing near.

selected.text: Therefore, as much as thou art able, be thou aflame - yet with wisdom - and be harmonious in thy melody - yet with moderation, lest it cause minds to be disturbed.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá encouraging the believer to be aflame yet with wisdom and harmonious yet with moderation; a memorable pairing of zeal and restraint.

selected.text: Yet with this steadfastness they must not let go of wisdom. As written before, they must not tear away veils and must be like angels and fairies, visible yet hidden
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asking the steadfast not to tear away veils but to be “visible yet hidden” like angels; a memorable image of steadfast discretion.

selected.text: In the Tablets We have commanded all to observe wisdom, and wisdom consists in such deeds and character as will cause the attraction and drawing nigh of the servants
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh defining wisdom as deeds and character that attract people and draw them near; a short definition that confirms the guide’s central theme.

selected.text: Thus it is manifest that tribulation in the path of God proffers to our lips the true chalice of His gifts and adversity is the outer form of His loving providence.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá teaching that tribulation in God’s path is the outer form of His loving providence; a strong statement on suffering.

selected.text: The language of the journal should be moderate and consideration should be shown as much as possible so as not to disturb thoughts or cause anxiety to anyone's heart
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá counseling that a journal’s language be moderate and considerate so as not to disturb anyone’s heart; a distinctive application of wisdom to publication.

selected.text: Great wisdom is needed lest what happened before should happen again. One must move with perfect wisdom. The ignorant people have been and are waiting to cause turmoil.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh calling for great wisdom lest past troubles recur, since the ignorant wait to cause turmoil; a lesson from experience.

selected.text: To teach by words requires the skill of a wise physician. He does not offer help to those who do not want treatment. Do not press help on those who do not need your help.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá comparing teaching to the skill of a wise physician who does not press help on those who do not want it; the opening’s practical image of respect for the listener.

selected.text: For the present this is in accord with wisdom. As we keep the latter, the former is left aside … My highest longing is to keep this fast, but wisdom must be considered
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that His longing is to keep the fast but wisdom must be considered; a personal example of judgment between duties.

selected.text: If a caravan wishes to traverse dangerous mountains and deserts, it must certainly be mindful of its protection and consider whatever means of preservation are necessary.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá comparing prudence to a caravan crossing dangerous mountains and deserts that must provide for its protection; a clear image of foresight.

selected.text: None is aware of the requirements of divine wisdom. The fruit of this ascension has been and remains within God's knowledge. It is not permitted to reveal it as it truly is.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh saying none is aware of the requirements of divine wisdom and the fruit of an ascension remains in God’s knowledge; a restrained word on loss.

selected.text: Such events and incidents are like the buzzing of a mosquito in an elephant's ear, and criticism from these souls is considered praise by the wise, as experience has shown.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá likening such incidents to a mosquito buzzing in an elephant’s ear and saying the wise count such criticism as praise; a memorable image of composure.

selected.text: When I have bad news for someone, I do not convey it to him openly, rather do I converse with him in such wise that when he heareth that news, my words bring comfort to him.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that He conveys bad news so that His words bring comfort when the news is heard; a distinctive example of caring speech.

selected.text: Observe carefully lest you fall into the snare of the treacherous and the false ones. Not every utterance is worthy of acceptance, nor is it permissible to trust every soul.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh warning against the snares of the treacherous, since not every utterance deserves acceptance nor every soul trust; continues the theme of checking claims.

selected.text: I bear witness, O my God, that in every one of Thy deeds there is wisdom upon wisdom, and mystery upon mystery, which Thou revealest in its time and manifesteth in its season.
selected.reason: Prayer of Bahá’u’lláh bearing witness that in every deed of God there is wisdom upon wisdom revealed in its time; a foundational statement of trust.

selected.text: Trust not every newcomer, nor believe every speaker. Make wisdom a lamp unto thyself and walk thereby in the darkness of the earth - then wilt thou be of those who are secure.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh bidding the believer trust not every newcomer and make wisdom a lamp to walk by in the darkness; a memorable image of discernment.

selected.text: You must be very moderate. Consider the taste of the public. This is the best policy. Moderation, moderation. You must speak and write in such a manner as not to offend anyone.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urging moderation and consideration of public taste so that speech and writing offend no one; practical counsel on the manner of speaking.

selected.text: wisdom is essential and caution necessary. Do not tear away veils. Speak with wisdom and do not converse with everyone. Converse with receptive souls and do not discuss doctrines
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advising not to converse with everyone but with receptive souls, and not to discuss doctrines; practical counsel on choosing hearers.

selected.text: Fix your gaze upon wisdom and hold fast unto its hem. Display not the pearls of divine knowledge before every ignorant one, and preserve them from thieves in the name of the Truth.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh bidding the believer not display the pearls of divine knowledge before every ignorant one; a memorable image of discretion.

selected.text: All your letters are pure truth, but affairs must revolve around the pivot of wisdom. Therefore, perhaps in view of the Most Great Compassion some accommodation will be made, but those accommodations are the essence of wisdom. Later you will observe this
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá affirming that a correspondent’s letters were pure truth but that affairs must revolve around the pivot of wisdom; a qualification that truth needs timing.

selected.text: Having regard to the need for wisdom, such a measure is not at present permissible, for the people of enmity and rancour lie in ambush, whilst the malevolent lurk in hidden corners.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying a measure was not permissible because the malevolent lay in ambush; an example of judging risk.

selected.text: If they desire to reform affairs, they must proceed with utmost calm and steadiness, and through good planning, without conflict and dispute, strive for what brings comfort and ease
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advising that those who would reform affairs proceed calmly, with good planning and without conflict; a practical model for change.

selected.text: God desired not thereby to extinguish His fire, but rather to kindle it, and in all that He doeth there is a wisdom which none comprehend save they who are endowed with clear vision.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh affirming that God sought to kindle, not extinguish, His fire, and that His wisdom is understood by those with clear vision; reframes hardship.

selected.text: If your coming does not cause any words, meaning it does not become a cause of fresh talk, there is no harm. However, if forbearance is possible, not moving at present is preferable.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying a visit is harmless if it causes no fresh talk, but forbearance is preferable if possible; an example of weighing consequences.

selected.text: A wise person acts thus - never wastes time, saying "time is a cutting sword," and with complete wisdom girds up his loins and finds no rest day or night, seeks not a moment's repose.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describing the wise person who wastes no time, since “time is a cutting sword”; shows wisdom as diligence as well as caution.

selected.text: sending letters was outwardly contrary to wisdom, as these regions were in turmoil due to the ongoing conflict, and the hand of investigation and inquiry was extended in every matter.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh explaining that sending letters was contrary to wisdom while the regions were in turmoil and under investigation; an example of correspondence shaped by danger.

selected.text: Divine wisdom hath been and shall ever be dominant and triumphant. One pure deed is like unto a lamp between heaven and earth - it showeth the way and guideth the heedless unto itself.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh comparing one pure deed to a lamp between heaven and earth that guides the heedless; carries the guide’s emphasis on deeds that persuade.

selected.text: but with perfect wisdom, since open teaching is not currently permitted in Egypt. With complete wisdom and the approval of the friends, teach whoever Jinab-i-Abu'l-Fadl deems advisable
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directing teaching in Egypt only with complete wisdom and the approval of the friends, since open teaching was not permitted; an example of a direction tied to place.

selected.text: Speech should be like the spring breezes, that the trees of being may thereby become verdant and flourishing. One word is like the vernal winds, while another is like the deadly simoom.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh likening speech to spring breezes that make the trees of being flourish, and another word to the deadly simoom; a vivid image of the effects of words.

selected.text: In all conditions, the exaltation of the Cause must be kept in view, and this cannot be achieved except through wisdom, and wisdom is not attainable except through meditation and patience.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh teaching that the exaltation of the Cause comes only through wisdom, and wisdom only through meditation and patience; names the inner disciplines from which wisdom grows.

selected.text: But keep this matter confidential, for if the women hear of it they will become extremely frightened at night and go mad. Only you and Isma'il Aqa should know of this and exercise caution.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asking that a frightening matter be kept from the women, lest they be terrified at night; an example of discretion out of care.

selected.text: write a brief response with utmost courtesy and gentleness, and "dispute with them in the kindliest manner" with a conciliatory tone, such that it absolutely does not cause him any offense
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advising a brief, courteous and conciliatory reply, disputing “in the kindliest manner” so as to give no offense; echoes the Qur’anic counsel the guide compares.

selected.text: And should anyone be kindled by this fire or be drawn by the call of the Chosen One, he must not transgress the wisdom which hath been sent down in the Tablet from the Pen of the All-Knowing.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh teaching that even one kindled by the fire of the Cause must not transgress the wisdom revealed in the Tablets; shows enthusiasm held within wisdom.

selected.text: Nonetheless, in the occurrence of this calamity a profound wisdom is hidden and concealed … Divine wisdom requireth this. In truth, it is the essence of loving-kindness and an unexcelled gift
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying a profound wisdom is hidden in a calamity and that it is the essence of loving-kindness; opens the turn to divine wisdom in suffering.

selected.text: According to His command, your honor should act with the utmost wisdom. It is not permissible to mention the Cause before the government and its officials, for this would be contrary to wisdom.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh forbidding mention of the Cause before the government and its officials as contrary to wisdom; a concrete direction under persecution.

selected.text: He too must act with wisdom, for some people are corrupt and have neither recognized nor understood the value of generosity, love, and true manliness. In all cases, one must hold fast to wisdom.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh counseling wisdom because some people have not understood the value of generosity, love and true manliness; a realistic reason for discretion.

selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that He speaks according to the time and the capacity of His listeners, as a father makes gurgling sounds for an infant; a memorable image of adapted speech.

selected.text: Affairs must be conducted with wisdom, and the meaning of wisdom is to be fervent and enthusiastic, without a moment's rest, while proceeding with reason and prudence, "By those who govern affairs
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá defining wisdom as fervent, untiring effort combined with reason and prudence; a definition that joins zeal to judgment.

selected.text: However, observance of wisdom is obligatory, for some were not and are not aware, clinging to conjecture and holding fast to suppositions, and these two are mighty barriers preventing the servants.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh calling wisdom obligatory because some cling to conjecture and supposition, mighty barriers for the servants; names the obstacles wisdom must reckon with.

selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asking that inner joy be joined to outward caution, lest the heedless misjudge the friends; shows wisdom shaping outward conduct.

selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: Regarding the journey of that beloved one and others, it was decided by lot and consent that, in accordance with wisdom, they should travel gradually, for if all travel at once it will not be free of talk.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh noting that travelers were to go gradually, by lot and consent, so their journey would not cause talk; a concrete example of practical wisdom.

selected.text: If thou wishest to mention thy Lord, mention Him with wisdom lest a sedition arise causing the feet of the weak to slip. selected.text: But divine wisdom contains hidden mysteries, and no one is aware of the concealed secret and protected mystery. Surely in this wandering there are thousands of liberations - its wisdom will become clear and evident later.

selected.text: O Jamal! The requirements of this age are different, and the requirements of divine wisdom are different. Therefore, the Pen of Will has paused in certain matters. In any case, they must observe wisdom and hold fast to it.

selected.text: The educative and reformative ideas must be introduced little by little according to the mental grasp and habits of the masses - so that they may adapt themselves to the new environment without any protest on their parts.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that reformative ideas must be introduced little by little according to people’s understanding and habits; a principle of gradual change.

selected.text: We counsel thee to observe wisdom, for the people are weak. The Lord, exalted be His glory, hath shown forbearance out of pure grace. Therefore must all be mindful of wisdom and treat mankind with kindliness and compassion.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh counseling wisdom because people are weak, citing God’s own forbearance and calling for kindliness and compassion; grounds human forbearance in divine grace.

selected.text: Beware, beware lest you depart from the wisdom which God has revealed in the Book. Deal with souls according to their capacity, treat the sick with their remedy, and dress the wound with a bandage that will heal it swiftly.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urging that souls be dealt with according to their capacity, the sick treated with their remedy and wounds dressed so they heal; a concise healing image of wisdom.

selected.text: However in Shiraz it must proceed with utmost wisdom and caution, so that strangers may never become aware … If not done thus, the base among the people shall arise to commit vile deeds and it shall cause dismay to hearts
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asking that matters in Shiraz proceed with utmost wisdom so that strangers never become aware; an example of a direction tied to place and danger.

selected.text: The holding of last night's meeting was done with wisdom and it produced great love … My discourses in various gatherings have been founded on principles that are in conformity with reality as well as with the utmost wisdom
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that a meeting held with wisdom produced great love and that His discourses joined reality with the utmost wisdom; shows wisdom bearing fruit in gatherings.

selected.text: In all our affairs we must use common sense. God has bestowed upon all of us reason that we might use it in our daily work and not hide it in the drawer. A sagacious man will wade through the stream only when it is fordable.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that God gave reason for daily use and that a sagacious man wades the stream only when it is fordable; a memorable image of common sense.

selected.text: All matters that come to pass are founded on divine wisdom. There is no motion or stillness that is not based on wisdom. Whatever outward causes may appear, they have spiritual causes behind them, and those causes are wisdom.
selected.reason: Reported words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that no motion or stillness is without wisdom and that outward causes have spiritual causes behind them; a substantive explanation.

selected.text: And in whatever place business is conducted, they must act with the utmost wisdom, for people are ignorant and the Persian consuls seize upon pretexts and engage in corruption and the seizure of properties, as they have done.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh asking that business be conducted with utmost wisdom because consuls seized pretexts to confiscate property; a distinctive application to economic life.

selected.text: Hold fast unto wisdom and grasp the hem of consultation. This is the binding command of God that hath been sent down and recorded in the Tablets from the Supreme Pen. Blessed is he who acteth accordingly; woe unto the heedless.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh bidding the friends hold fast to wisdom and grasp the hem of consultation as God’s binding command; joins wisdom and consultation.

selected.text: Thus, a measure must be taken to somewhat ease and lighten the calamity, lest these afflictions, God forbid, continue … Wisdom is certainly required in divine commands, consideration is necessary and preservation is essential
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urging measures to lighten a calamity and saying wisdom, consideration and preservation are required; a practical response to suffering.

selected.text: Man must take a lesson from divine actions and deeds for God suffers a tree to grow a long time before it attains to perfection.  He is able to make a tree grow to fruition in an instant, but wisdom requires a gradual development
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá drawing a lesson from God letting a tree grow slowly though He could make it bear fruit at once, since wisdom requires gradual development; a memorable image of patience.

selected.text: However, in all circumstances they must observe wisdom. O people of Baha and Dal! Hearken unto the counsel of the Wronged One. In all circumstances be mindful of wisdom and hold fast unto that which is conducive to reconciliation.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh calling the people of Bahá to be mindful of wisdom in all circumstances and hold fast to what conduces to reconciliation; joins wisdom to reconciliation.

selected.text: It is incumbent upon thee, however, to act with the utmost discretion, for men are ignorant and prejudiced and seek to stir sedition and mischief. Wherefore, saith Christ in the Gospel: 'Tell not the Pharisees and inform them not.'
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urging discretion among the prejudiced and citing Christ’s words, “Tell not the Pharisees”; a distinctive scriptural support for discretion.

selected.text: Nevertheless, it is observed that some have strayed from the straight path of wisdom, which is the foundation of God's Holy City. For instance, they give meat instead of milk to the infant, and poison instead of healing to the sick.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh describing those who stray from wisdom as giving meat instead of milk to infants and poison instead of healing to the sick; vivid images of speech that ignores capacity.

selected.text: Some who claim to love God in various regions are deprived of both deeds and wisdom, but God is the Concealer, the All-Knowing. Many times has this exalted Word been mentioned: "Believe not every speaker, and trust not every newcomer
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh noting that some who claim to love God lack both deeds and wisdom, repeating “Believe not every speaker, and trust not every newcomer”; reinforces discernment.

selected.text: We have enjoined wisdom upon Our servants lest there occur that which would disturb the hearts of humanity … Verily he who speaketh for the sake of God and holdeth fast to wisdom, his words will influence the hearts of the heedless
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh saying that one who speaks for God’s sake and holds to wisdom will influence the hearts of the heedless; joins sincerity and wisdom in effective speech.

selected.reason: Tablet of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying that one who knows a wisdom should explain it and leave the listener free to decide, without being disheartened if it is not accepted; anchors the opening test of the hearer’s freedom.

selected.text: If there is some delay in granting permission for some to attend at this blessed spot, this is due to the wisdom set forth in the Book … Therefore, wisdom requires that this land remain thus for a while until some calm is achieved
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explaining that delays in permission to visit were due to wisdom until calm was achieved; an example of patience in pilgrimage.

selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh saying all are commanded to wisdom and love and that conduct pleasing to the consul would be most fitting; a distinctive application to relations with officials.

selected.text: However, in all circumstances wisdom must be observed, and one must deal with people with kindness and compassion, for they are weak - had they known, they would have circled round the Countenance. The heedless people need wise counselors.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh asking that people be treated with kindness and compassion because they are weak, and saying the heedless need wise counselors; joins wisdom with compassion.

selected.text: This concealment is greater than open acknowledgment, for therein lies infinite wisdom. Among other things, he can engage in service, establish bonds of fellowship with everyone, and with the utmost spirituality make strangers into friends.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying that one believer’s concealment was greater than open acknowledgment, since it let him serve and befriend strangers; a distinctive account of discretion’s fruit.

selected.text: But one must be forbearing and considerate. No harsh word should be spoken about anyone. The Covenant-breakers should be left to the Blessed Beauty. selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá counseling forbearance, no harsh word about anyone and the gentle presentation of proofs even amid opposition; shows wisdom governing speech under strain.

selected.text: But this must be done with wisdom, for today in God's sight the observance of wisdom taketh precedence over all deeds. All must hold fast unto it, lest there occur that which would extinguish the divine fire and cause hearts to be troubled.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh saying that observance of wisdom takes precedence over all deeds, lest the divine fire be extinguished; a strong statement of wisdom’s priority.

selected.text: We have commanded all to wisdom, and they who are endued with insight must look to the Command of God and not act according to their own will. They must carry out that which they have been commanded and abandon that which hath been forbidden.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh teaching that those with insight look to God’s command rather than their own will; guards wisdom from becoming self-justification.

selected.reason: Tablet of Bahá’u’lláh describing the wisdom revealed in the Tablets as deeds that draw people near and enlighten the peoples; a second foundational definition tied to conduct.

selected.text: Now regarding wisdom, it is not time for teachers to request from the government reduction of half their travel expenses, or exemption from government fees for Mashriqu'l-Adhkar endowments. Wisdom does not require this now - the time will come.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá saying it is not yet time for teachers to seek government concessions, though the time will come; an example of wisdom about timing requests.

selected.text: The sage hath said: "Either make not friends with elephant-keepers, or build a house fit for an elephant." Praise be to God, it appeareth that you have built a house worthy of an eagle and befitting the Phoenix of the dawning-place of the righteous

selected.text: This announcement should be given forth with wisdom, and not in haste, for it would be a cause of stirring up. When ye find a soul manifesting a demand for Truth, then ye may give this to him, that he may be informed of the rudiments of the Cause.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directing that an announcement be given with wisdom and not in haste, to those who show a demand for truth; shows judgment about readiness.

selected.text: Those souls who in this Day have quaffed the sealed wine from the hand of the Self-Subsisting Sovereign must fix their gaze upon wisdom and hold fast to the cord of unity, for these two are the cause and means for the exaltation of the Cause of God.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh naming wisdom and unity as the two means for the exaltation of the Cause; pairs wisdom with fellowship.

selected.text: All men are commanded to observe wisdom, and forbidden to engage in mischief, strife and contention; yet should aught befall, then with perfect resignation must they direct their steps unto the scene of sacrifice in the path of the Incomparable Friend
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh joining the command to wisdom and the prohibition of strife with resignation to sacrifice should anything befall; a strong statement of courage and restraint together.

selected.text: This is why all are occupied with wisdom - that is, with whatever preserves the commanding self. If they had drunk a drop from the cup of love, they would surely burn a hundred thousand wisdoms with fire and cast a hundred thousand prudences to the wind.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh contrasting a wisdom that merely preserves the self with love that would burn a hundred thousand wisdoms; the guide’s key warning that caution can go too far.

selected.text: It is incumbent upon you, however, to act with the utmost discretion and not to rend the veil asunder, for the enemy, whether he be near or afar, lieth in wait and stirreth the negligent to arise against His Holiness Baha'u'llah. Be ye prudent, be ye discreet.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urging discretion and not rending the veil because the enemy lies in wait; carries the theme of restraint under danger.

selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh asking that the loved ones be counseled not to believe every speaker or trust every claimant, and to safeguard what must be safeguarded; reinforces checking claims.

selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh telling an aging believer that hardships are permitted only within bearable limits; a personal application of moderation in service.

selected.text: This point is clear and evident. Some believe that wisdom is the knowledge of the realities of things, and whoever attains this station will possess lofty stations. Some maintain that wisdom is the science of association with people and treating servants of God with moderation. Others have said that wisdom is theology according to the principles of previous philosophers. Likewise, they have said wisdom is the knowledge of substances and accidents, as well as astronomy and the like. Some have said wisdom is the knowledge of livelihood in this world. Some assert that wisdom is the knowledge of principles. Some souls maintain that wisdom pertains to matters of justice, which is and will be giving each their due right. Each group, according to their understanding, has presented proofs and evidence for each of what has been mentioned, which if detailed would add to weariness. Glory be to Him Who spoke this supreme word: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of God," for the fear and awe of God restraineth man from whatsoever causeth abasement and degradation of the human station, and aideth him in that which leadeth to elevation and glory. The wise man avoideth shameful deeds, for he beholdeth punishment in their wake. The pavilion of world order is upheld upon two pillars: Reward and Punishment.
